(Kitco News) – China’s 2026 gold imports could be double those of last year, and will set the high-water mark for the 2020s to date, while silver prices are approaching a key test that could determine the gray metal’s near-term direction, according to precious metals analysts at Heraeus.
In their latest update, the analysts noted that China’s gold imports have already exceeded 2025 totals in 2026. “China imported 142 tonnes of gold in August, taking imports during the first eight months of the year to 1,141 tonnes, 72% higher than the 663 tonnes imported over the same period last year, and higher than the 940 tonnes imported during the whole of 2025,” they wrote. “The strong inflows come despite historically high gold prices and reflect continued investment demand, while Chinese jewellery demand remains comparatively weak. These non-monetary imports are separate from purchases by the People’s Bank of China, which added a further 20 tonnes to its official reserves in August.”
“If Chinese gold imports maintain this pace through the rest of 2026, they will total ~1,700 tonnes, which would represent the highest amount this decade.”
Australia’s gold mine production continued to rise in fiscal year 2025-26 as historically high prices continue to support the mining sector. “Australia produced 303 tonnes of gold up to the end of its financial year in June, broadly in line with its long-run production rate of around 300 tonnes p.a.,” the analysts said. “Output improved at most operations during the June quarter, while several smaller producers also began production. The 303 tonnes produced in Australia account for around 8% of total mined gold supply, which was 3,822 tonnes in 2025.”
Heraeus said Indonesia is proposing a scheme to incentivize privately held gold stocks to be invested into the formal financial system. “The government estimates that households hold around 1,800 tonnes of gold outside formal investment channels and has asked state-owned institutions to encourage around 20% of this metal, equivalent to roughly 360 tonnes, into bullion-banking and financial products,” they wrote. “The initiative is aimed at turning privately held metal into deposits, collateral and other financial assets, deepening the domestic bullion market and potentially increasing the amount of household wealth circulating through the financial system.”
The analysts also warned that India’s weak monsoon will likely depress rural gold demand during this year’s festival and wedding season – and rural demand represents over 50% of the country’s total bullion consumption. “Monsoon rainfall was around 15% below its long-run average by late September, presenting a downside risk to gold demand due to the potential of lower crop yields to impact rural incomes,” they said. “Historical analysis by the World Gold Council suggests that a 1% increase in rainfall relative to the average is associated with a 0.2% increase in gold demand, implying that this year’s rainfall deficit could represent a modest headwind. Indian gold demand totalled 768 tonnes in 2025, roughly 15% of global demand.”
Spot gold was continuing to test session lows early in the North American session, and last traded at $4,142.30 for a loss of 3.33% on the daily chart.
Turning to silver, Heraeus analysts noted that the renewed strength of the U.S. dollar has driven silver prices to a key inflection point.
“Silver prices dropped below $65/oz last week as the dollar index rose back above 101.0, towards its yearly highs,” they noted. “This leaves silver at an important level. A renewed rally back towards $70/oz despite a rising dollar, a hawkish Federal Reserve and rising bond yields could signal a confirmation of a potential bottoming process. However, if silver falls back below $60/oz, this could be the sign of a continuation of the bearish downtrend, marked by lower highs and lower lows, in which silver has been stuck since its late January peak.”
The analysts wrote that the 10-year Treasury yield’s rise to 5.22% and the 10-year Treasury Inflation-Protected Security (TIPS) real yield hitting 2.8% indicates that the Federal Reserve’s 25 basis point rate hike in September was not enough to reassure markets.
“The rise in real yields alongside nominal yields is particularly significant for precious metals, indicating that the sell-off in Treasuries has not been driven solely by higher inflation expectations, but also by investors demanding a higher inflation-adjusted return, consistent with the anticipation that monetary policy could remain tighter for longer,” they said. “This comes as Brent crude remains around $100/bbl, and despite renewed talks between the US and Iran, a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz does not appear imminent.”
And Indian silver imports spiked higher in August after several months of weak inflows. “India imported 15.5 moz of silver in August, the first time since February that monthly imports have topped 10 moz and 36% higher than the 11.4 moz imported in August 2025,” the analysts wrote. “Despite the strong monthly recovery, imports remain weak for the year as a whole, with an estimated 75.6 moz imported during January-August, 24% less than the 99.1 moz imported over the same period last year.”
“The rebound follows several months of unusually low imports after the licensing requirements introduced in May complicated the import process and high silver prices reduced demand, they said. “The upswing in August suggests that physical inflows are beginning to normalise, although year-to-date imports remain well below last year’s levels.”
Silver prices were also trading just above their earlier session lows on Monday morning after dipping below $61 per ounce around 5 am ET.

In today’s newsletter: New details suggest there is a counter-narrative to how events unfolded at the airbase used by the US
Good morning. Vehicles suspected of carrying explosives zipping across Britain, entirely unbeknownst to authorities, is a disconcerting prospect.
Initially, it seemed precisely this had occurred in Gloucestershire early on Sunday. A major attack on RAF Fairford appeared to have been scuppered by “pure luck”, a local farmer said, after she noticed suspicious vans and masked men on an otherwise deserted country lane. Had she not tipped off police, the vigilant villager believes the five men arrested on terror offences would not have been apprehended. That account prompted questions about whether police and security services had been caught off guard.
Bu new details emerging suggest there are competing, if not conflicting, versions of how events unfolded in the Cotswolds this weekend. So what exactly happened in the early hours of Sunday morning? In today’s First Edition, we’ll explore this, and some other unanswered questions, with the help of Guardian international security correspondent Jason Burke . Before that, this morning’s headlines.
Energy | Andy Burnham will take his first major step to putting Britain’s utility companies into public control when, at the Labour conference, he announces a new government-backed body to invest in the electricity grid.
Immigration | Home secretary Shabana Mahmood has signalled she is considering watering down her plans to make it harder for foreign workers to claim permanent residence in the UK, amid growing demands for a U-turn from cabinet colleagues and unions.
AI | Two of the “godfathers” of modern AI and senior executives at OpenAI and Anthropic have warned governments to prepare for an AI “intelligence explosion”, which they say could be the most consequential technological development in history.
Petrol | The price of diesel on UK forecourts has hit an all-time high average of 199.18p a litre, as the conflict in the Middle East continues to drive the cost of fuel to record levels.
Ebola | A senior member of the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s ruling party was beaten to death on Sunday after appearing on a radio programme to raise awareness about the Ebola outbreak, a party representative has said.
In the early hours of Sunday, a farmer from the village of Whelford was travelling home from a party along quiet rural roads. She was about to drop off a friend, while her husband dozed in the passenger seat. Around 1am, however, she encountered three vans “parked in a really weird fan shape” blocking the path to her farm, close to RAF Fairford, an airbase operated by the US air force.
Forced to turn around, she then described seeing “a large group of hooded and masked men” at a nearby junction, who quickly dispersed.
After a failed attempt to contact the Ministry of Defence, she phoned the police at 1.36am and posted in the local residents’ WhatsApp group. Roughly 10 minutes later, armed officers were on the scene. Five men were arrested 300 metres from the base’s perimeter, first under the Explosives Act, and subsequently also on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. All five – UK nationals from London aged between 23 and 25 – were released on bail yesterday. In interviews, the farmer, who has remained anonymous, reiterated her belief that her tip off “foiled whatever plans” were unfolding. “I am absolutely staggered that it was left to me, as a member of the public, to see and report this,” she said.
That the high-security site was so exposed, and that the vans suspected of carrying explosives in its vicinity went totally unnoticed, has since raised questions. While thanking the farmer for her efforts, defence secretary Wes Streeting was quick to cast doubt on her assertions, hinting that UK security services were aware and that her account only offered “a partial picture”.
Donald Trump has claimed the US and UK agencies worked together and had the five men “under view for a long time”, adding the suspects “were looking to do big damage to our fort, and working with the British worked out great”.
The farmer acknowledged there had been “activity” by what she “assumed were plain-clothed police officers” in the area in recent days. Another local told the BBC that while walking their dog early on Saturday evening they were stopped by armed police and told to return home.
Gloucestershire constabulary said they were first alerted to the suspicious vans at 12.45am on Sunday – almost an hour before the farmer’s 999 call. Counter-terror police have confirmed the three vehicles had been travelling overnight and been subject to extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts. It is now understood that the material found inside them was not viable explosives, but police have said the investigation is continuing.
And then there’s the expeditious nature of the response: the speed with which armed officers and police helicopters arrived at a rural location in the middle of the night appears improbable.
Questions around the arrests
Police are still working to establish motive. Yesterday afternoon, the head of UK National Counter Terrorism Policing, Laurence Taylor, confirmed it may have been the work of proxies, or individuals working on behalf of a foreign state.
On Monday night, US secretary of state Marco Rubio told Fox News that a foreign actor was involved in the suspected plot, but provided no evidence for his claims.
Iran is the centre of speculation, having explicitly stated it considers RAF Fairford “a legitimate target”. Yesterday, the Iranian embassy said it “categorically rejects” any involvement.
Used by the US military for decades, RAF Fairford’s two-mile long runway was specially constructed by the Americans to allow long-range bombers to take off and land. Fairford has played a significant role in Trump’s war on Iran; since former prime minister Keir Starmer allowed the US to use UK bases in its assaults, bomb-laden American B-52 and B-1 planes have regularly been spotted taking off. The airbase is one of only two available to the US in Europe that can facilitate these operations, after Spain, France, Italy and Switzerland rejected similar American requests.
“Most observers and analysts would place Iran at the top of the list of potential suspects here,” Jason Burke, the Guardian’s international security correspondent, tells me, “though we have very little in the way of information to work on, so it’s entirely possible an altogether different scenario is at play.”
As for the five suspects, their being British nationals is likely of little help when determining who may be behind the plot. “The Iranian modus operandi – borrowing a leaf from the Russian playbook – relies on using local hires,” Jason says. “Instead of deploying their own intelligence operatives, they recruit low-grade agents on the ground, some of whom may not fully realise what they are involved in.”
Since the US-Israel war on Iran began, a series of UK security incidents have been linked with Iran. Earlier this month, a man and a woman were arrested after raids on homes in north London on suspicion of assisting Iran’s foreign intelligence service. In March, four Jewish community ambulances were destroyed in an arson attack – counter-terror police explored the possible involvement of Iranian proxies, though aside from a reference to a “terrorist connection”, no mention of Iran was made by prosecutors in court when four men admitted responsibility.
Similar suggestions have been made about tens of other antisemitic attacks in the UK and Europe – Iran’s embassy in the UK has denied any involvement.

After President Donald Trump rolled out the red carpet for his summit with China’s Xi Jinping last week, the U.S. and China agreed to move toward lower tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods in each direction. China’s side covers 1,619 U.S. products—stretching from beef and seafood to cosmetics and medical gear—but it leaves out a politically sensitive import: commodity soybeans.
While seed soybeans, soybean flour, and by-products from soybean processing made the cut for tariff relief, the raw soybeans American farmers sell in bulk to China—the ones at the heart of U.S-China farm tensions—did not.
Soybeans are one of the country’s biggest agricultural exports, and China is the most important buyer. The U.S. exported $16.5 billion worth of soybeans last year, making soybeans the second-largest agricultural export after corn, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture . China buys more soybeans than every other country because it has limited arable land.
That dependence has made soybeans vulnerable to swings in U.S.-China trade policy. In the years before the first Trump trade war in 2018, the American Soybean Association estimated 28% of all U.S. soybean production was shipped to China. When Beijing then imposed a 25% retaliatory tariff on U.S. soybeans in 2018, the USDA estimated farmers absorbed $9.4 billion in soybean losses, costing Iowa $1.2 billion and Illinois $1.3 billion.
The Midwest bears the brunt of this pressure. Illinois and Iowa are the country’s two largest soybean producers, followed by Minnesota, Indiana, and Nebraska. North and South Dakota, Missouri, and Ohio are also major growers. Soybeans are traded in export and national markets, so weaker Chinese demand can hurt farmers by driving down the cash prices they receive at local grain facilities.
That helps explain why Trump focused on soybeans in his dealmaking with Beijing. In November, he struck a deal with Xi under which China committed to buying at least 25 million metric tons of soybeans in 2026, 2027, and 2028. After he met Xi in May, the first time a U.S. president visited China since 2017, the White House announced China agreed to buy at least $17 billion in agricultural products on top of those prior soybean commitments.
For all of soybeans’ importance to American farmers, China has another supplier: Brazil.
Unlike with products such as beef, whose quality varies depending on the country of origin, bulk soybeans are interchangeable and ultimately end up crushed in troughs for livestock feed, according to Ker Gibbs, former president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai. “They go into pig feed, so it’s not like the pigs are really gonna see a big difference between American soybeans and Brazilian soybeans,” he told Fortune .
Brazil had already overtaken the U.S. as China’s largest soybean supplier over a decade ago, but recent trade tensions have widened the gap. USDA said 71% of China’s soybean imports came from Brazil , and its agricultural attaché in Beijing reported last year that Brazil’s share had continued to grow “at the expense of the United States,” helped by cheaper prices.
“They definitely want to keep Brazil warm, and so they don’t want to suddenly shift everything over to the U.S.,” Gibbs told Fortune about China excluding commodity soybeans from the list. “They’re leaving the door half closed.”
Leaving raw soybeans outside the tariff relief package also gives Beijing a holstered weapon, according to Usha Haley, a professor at Wichita State University who has studied Chinese trade strategy.
“That gives China a bargaining chip for subsequent talks, and, of course, this is about leverage,” Haley told Fortune . “They offer enough to demonstrate that they are moving on things, that they are present, but they always hold something back economically and politically for the next round.”
China doesn’t need to stop buying U.S. soybeans entirely for that pressure to work, having bought 1 million tons of them ahead of the Trump-Xi summit.
“Commercial purchasing and negotiating leverage can operate simultaneously,” Haley said. She ‘said’ China just has to keep access to its soybean market uncertain and expensive for farmers operating on thin margins. “Uncertainty also has a cost.”

Antonia is a reporter based in Kyiv who covers Ukraine and Russia. She was shortlisted for Best Early Career Journalist in the Freelance Journalist Awards 2025
Robert Brovdi sets a box of Fortnum & Mason tea bags down next to a digital counter.
The white number reads 167: the Russian soldiers – or, as Mr Brovdi calls them, “worms” – killed that day.
The rate of attrition is intensifying rapidly, the commander of Ukraine’s drone forces and one of the chief architects of modern warfare says.
His troops have seen a 25 per cent increase in Russian casualties since August as more of the Kremlin’s foot soldiers approach the front lines .
It is his view, shared by Ukrainian military intelligence, that Vladimir Putin will imminently launch a fresh round of mobilisation to break the current stalemate.
Some 300,000 will arrive in the coming months, he estimates, in an attempt to capture the rest of the Donbas region.
“Putin will send his serfs onto the front line, and they will drop dead in even greater numbers than right now,” he says, confident that his forces can pick them off from above as the trees and bushes lose their foliage.
He picks up the counter, which has now reached 185.
“By the time we had exchanged a few sentences, 18 more b-----ds have already ended their stories in the ‘special military operation’.”
He boasts that his forces are now killing the equivalent of one enemy battalion per day.
“We are ready to welcome these limitless portions of stewed meat.”
Our interview takes place in an underground command post at a secret location in eastern Ukraine.
A team from The Telegraph was driven there on the morning Ukraine launched its largest-ever drone attack on Moscow.
It was the final day of elections in Russia, after which many experts predicted Putin would escalate his war on Ukraine and, in some respects , Europe.
The bunker is dimly lit by a bank of screens on the walls showing live footage recorded by drones hovering over the 745 miles of front line.
The tea bags are another feature, one he will turn to later to make a point about British drone prowess – or its lack thereof.
Before the war, the head of Ukraine’s unmanned systems forces and founder of the elite “Magyar’s Birds” drone unit was a wealthy international grain trader and art patron with no military experience to speak of.
An ethnic Hungarian from Uzhhorod in western Ukraine, with the call sign Magyar – “the Hungarian” – Mr Brovdi enlisted in Ukraine’s territorial defence just before the war began. Later, while serving in the 206th territorial defence battalion, he became one of the first to envision the role that drones could play in the conflict.
Mr Brovdi deployed rudimentary commercial drones to reconnoitre Russian positions after he’d bought an unmanned aerial vehicle ( UAV ) as a gift for his son.
The breakthrough, which took place in summer 2022 in Kherson, saw him sending coordinates to a nearby artillery team. But it was not long before his troops were experimenting with attaching their own munitions to the drones, which they also began manufacturing themselves.
Those improvised experiments, borne largely of desperation and a lack of resources, would prove to be the crucible from which Ukraine’s sophisticated drone warfare apparatus emerged.
The commander’s mordant wit and distinctive parlance (Russian soldiers are khrobaky , worms or bugs, while Ukrainians are pest-controlling “birds”) have transformed him into an icon of the war effort. But he has also brought to the battlefield the same mathematical and business acumen that once served him in the world of commerce, turning Ukraine’s drone strategy into a rigorous data-led exercise.
His pivotal role has also turned him into a priority target for the Kremlin. To meet him requires a series of precautions, starting with a journey to an undisclosed location in a blacked-out van after being stripped of all electronic devices, followed by a descent into the underground command post.
On a wall at its entrance, the sleek black carcass of a real Shahed drone, gutted for its parts, is mounted like the spoils of a hunt. Inside, hundreds of live first-person feeds from the battlefield line the walls on vast screens. Combing the terrain from above, lone Russian troops are stalked through the landscape and their vehicles obliterated. An electronic ledger on the wall tallies the number of enemy soldiers, artillery and weapons systems destroyed in real time.
The feeds are interspersed with maps of St Petersburg and Moscow, the latter visited only hours earlier by hundreds of Ukrainian drones – an explosive closing ceremony for Russia’s three-day parliamentary elections.
Despite the scale and ferocity of the nighttime attacks, Mr Brovdi showed no trace of fatigue. He dons a black cap embroidered with one of his slogans – Moskva lyazhe , roughly “Moscow will fall” – as he expounds on the role of his forces’ “deep strikes” in bringing the war home to Russia.
“In all of its previous wars, Russia waged them in such a way that its civilian population did not feel directly affected by the war,” says the commander.
“In 2026, this situation has been changed by our freedom-loving Ukrainian ‘birds’. Deep operations have effectively destroyed the concept of having a safe rear across the entire European part of Russia.”
This year, expanded strikes on Russia’s oil industry and commercial targets such as warehouses belonging to e-commerce giants Ozon and Wildberries have reached as far as 3,000km – almost 1,900 miles – from the Ukrainian border.
Kyiv claims that its attacks, which have hit all but five of Russia’s 32 biggest oil refineries, have sent total oil refining capacity plummeting by 45 per cent, offering some leverage to its leaders in talks. Last week, Donald Trump prematurely announced a limited energy truce on both sides, though Russia has refused such a moratorium.
“The appearance in 2026, however illusory, of even a faint prospect of a dialogue about an energy truce is the direct result of the Ukrainian ‘birds’ and Ukrainian pilots,” Mr Brovdi says.
But when it comes to the prospects of the broader US-Ukraine-Russia negotiating track, recently revived with consecutive trips to Moscow and Kyiv by the US president’s envoys, he harbours few hopes: “From a military point of view, I do not believe in an end to the war even if a ceasefire agreement is reached.”
Evidence of this, perhaps, is Russia’s escalating aerial campaign against Ukrainian cities far behind the front line, targeting energy infrastructure, logistics and civilian commercial targets. During the last two months, Moscow has deployed wave after wave of jet-powered drones against Kyiv, often spanning much of the day and night, and keeping the capital under near-constant air raids.
Ukraine has struggled to defend itself against the drones, which move significantly faster and at higher altitudes than earlier generations and have struck petrol stations, warehouses, border crossings, railway infrastructure, depots, postal services and more.
Mr Brovdi said that it was natural that each side would occasionally gain the upper hand in weaponry, and that Ukraine would develop new tools to defend itself.
“This technological war involves cycles of open windows when one side gets hold of some new technology and the other takes counter-measures in a short period of time,” he said.
“The jet-powered Shahed represents the window in the cycle that the Ukrainian side has not yet closed,” he admitted, yet added that counter-measures were already being deployed after rapid work by engineers.
“They work in close cooperation with front-line troops and have successfully started to launch jet-powered anti-Shahed systems and shoot down drones,” the commander said.

articles.content_orig:
Hi, this is Evelyn, writing to you from Beijing. Welcome to the latest edition of The China Connection — a snapshot of what I'm seeing and hearing from local businesses.
Now that the second Trump-Xi summit of the year is over, it's clear the show was aimed more at home than reaching tangible outcomes . Is agreeing to talk enough?
The $30 billion tariff rollback released Monday morning Beijing time reads like the perfect shopping list.
American consumers get to buy cheaper curtains, sports equipment and Christmas lights. Chinese get a discount on U.S. beef, soymeal and other agricultural products. American ice cream is even on the list.
It's the most detailed outcome so far of the summit last week between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, D.C.
The official readouts otherwise did not make much headway on major issues, beyond agreeing to keep talking and extending a trade truce — which keeps tariffs lower and rare earths flowing — for another two months.
"Both sides are signaling not to each other, but to their own sides," Cameron Johnson, Shanghai-based senior partner of consultancy Tidal Wave Solutions, told me on Monday.
"The reality is neither side can do a whole lot in technology without the other," he said, "so it's important that both sides signal that to their own apparatus: It's OK to have some competition."
Over the weekend, The Information reported , citing sources, that the Chinese government has signaled it could allow some domestic companies like ByteDance and Alibaba to buy Nvidia's chip built for high-end professional computers. While the U.S. has agreed to let Nvidia sell some less advanced chips to China, there have been few signs that Chinese companies were allowed to buy them amid Beijing's push for self-sufficiency.
In Beijing's readout of talks with Trump, Xi acknowledged "healthy" competition with the U.S. was possible, without confrontation. Both countries have planned discussions on AI in coming weeks.
"I think the top priority for both leaders is to maintain domestic stability and prosperity," said Hai Zhao, a director of international political studies at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, a state-affiliated think tank.
"And if the two top economies are stable and growing, that is, I think, the best contribution to global stability and prosperity," he told me on Friday.
Both countries are seeing growth concentrated in tech-related sectors, also known as the "K-shaped" economy. AI's development poses the same risks to jobs and national security.
The U.S. and Chinese readouts also signaled some alignment on limiting Iran's nuclear weapon capabilities, and agreed "no country or institution can be allowed to impose tolls on international waterways."
"Even though China [and the] U.S. may have different strategic goals in different regions, however, from time to time, they share the same mutual interest," Zhao said, pointing to the need for stable trade flows through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.
"In many ways they can working towards the same goal by not necessarily working with each other," he said. "I call this passive cooperation."
Zhao also hopes U.S. and European scrutiny on China's exports can be resolved by encouraging Chinese companies to invest.
While the U.S. and China have released more details on the Board of Trade, less is yet known about the Board of Investment.
The question is whether it will get enough airtime in a packed political calendar.
Trump faces the midterm elections in early November. Xi will oversee a plenary meeting in late October aimed at unifying the ruling Communist Party of China. The two presidents are also planning to meet: in Shenzhen in November and in Miami in December.
"After eight turbulent years spanning trade war 1.0 to trade war 2.0, signs of stability carry real weight for domestic audiences and entrepreneurs, who are concerned about external environment," Macquarie's Chief China Economist, Larry Hu, said in a report Sunday.
"In reality," he said, "the U.S.–China relationship also anchors much of China's broader diplomacy with the rest of the world."

articles.content_orig:
The United Arab Emirates has confirmed that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met with President Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan during a visit to the country over the weekend.
The confirmation late on Monday came a day after the Israeli leader made the secret trip to the UAE capital, Abu Dhabi. The visit came a month before Israeli elections and amid controversy over reports alleging that Bin Zayed, known as MBZ, had warned Netanyahu that a major Hamas operation was likely just ahead of the attack on southern Israel on October 7, 2023.
“During the meeting, the two sides discussed bilateral relations between the UAE and Israel and ways to strengthen and develop them,” the official Emirates News Agency, WAM, reported on Monday. The meeting was earlier reported in the Israeli press.
Palestinian fighters killed at least 1,195 people in southern Israel during the attack and took around 250 captive. Israel’s response developed into a genocidal war on Gaza, in which at least 73,669 Palestinians have been killed.
Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported on September 9 that the UAE president spoke to Netanyahu on the phone about 10 days before the attack, warning him of a threat made by then-Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar that he was preparing a “huge surprise”.
Bin Zayed had previously alerted Israel’s Shin Bet intelligence agency, the Haaretz report said.
Netanyahu’s office has denied that the prime minister received information ahead of the attacks.
Netanyahu said the following day that he would sue Haaretz, calling its report “fabricated” and “politically motivated”.
Relations between Israel and the UAE have warmed since the UAE signed the US-brokered Abraham Accords in 2020, which normalised ties between Israel and a number of Arab states.
United States Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee said in May that Israel had deployed Iron Dome air defence batteries and personnel to the UAE to help defend against potential Iranian attacks.
Israel’s Channel 12 first reported on Netanyahu’s trip to the UAE over the weekend. articles.title_orig: Tennessee to execute a woman for first time in 200 years after governor denies clemency
articles.title_zh: Tennessee to execute a woman for first time in 200 years after governor denies clemency
articles.content_orig:
Lawyers for Christa Pike, 50, convicted of killing classmate in Knoxville in 1995, ask supreme court to grant stay
Christa Pike, a woman who was convicted of murder 30 years ago, is set to be put to death on Wednesday after her request for clemency was denied by Tennessee governor Bill Lee on Monday. If the execution goes through, she will be the first woman executed in the state in 200 years.
Pike, who is now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend, who was 17 at the time, killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmate at Knoxville Job Corps in 1995.
The case received widespread attention because of the brutality of the killing, the ages of the people involved, and because a satanic symbol was carved into the victim’s body.
Pike was convicted of first-degree murder the following year and sentenced to death, making her the youngest woman to be put on death row in modern US history. Since her sentence, her history as a victim of sexual abuse and mental health challenges has come to light.
As her execution date approached, civil rights groups like the ACLU and Amnesty International have called on the public to reach out to the governor’s office to ask that he take Pike off of death row.
But Lee declined to halt her execution.
“After deliberate consideration of Christa Gail Pike’s request for clemency and after a thorough review of the case, I am upholding the sentence of the State of Tennessee and do not plan to intervene,” he said in a statement .
In response to Lee’s decision, Pike’s attorneys said that they were “deeply saddened and heartbroken” by the governor’s decision and that through this choice the state is dismissing decades of research about the amount of responsibility an 18-year-old – especially one with severe trauma – should bear for their criminal actions.
“Throughout her childhood, Christa was failed by people and institutions that should have shown her care and meaningful intervention,” Pike’s attorneys said in a statement. “The 18-year-old girl suffering from severe mental illness and near-debilitating trauma no longer exists. Christa is a 50-year-old remorseful woman who understands her actions, receives proper treatment for her mental illness, and provides for and guides fellow incarcerated women.”
Pike’s attorneys have also asked the supreme court to stay the execution.
Assistant federal defender Stephen Ferrell said Pike was sexually abused starting from when she was a toddler and that she was raped at 11 and 17. He said Pike’s lawyers at the penalty phase of her trial did not present the jury with what he said was critical information about her past or argue that her age should be a consideration.
Pike , who has never denied her role in Slemmer’s killing, was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.
“I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime,” Pike said in a statement included in her clemency petition.
Ferrell said more is known today about adolescent brain development and that Pike’s death sentence is an outlier. He noted that Pike’s boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, who was 17 at the time, was sentenced to life with the possibility of parole because of his age. He was denied parole last year. A third teen admitted to being an accessory and received probation.
May Martinez, Slemmer’s mother, told the Associated press that her daughter volunteered with the Special Olympics, loved roller skating and wanted to pursue a career in computers.
“She was easygoing. She was a computer geek to begin with. She and my husband would build and tear apart the computers constantly,” Martinez told the outlet. “She trusted everybody, and that was her downfall.”
The last woman executed in Tennessee was in 1820, according to the Death Penalty Information Center . Martin Eve, charged with being an accessory to murder, was executed by hanging.
Most recently, Missouri in 2023 executed Amber McLaughlin, a transgender woman, for a 2003 killing, in what is believed to be the first execution of a transgender woman in the US.
In 2021, the federal government executed Lisa Montgomery, marking the first time in nearly seven decades that the US government has put a female inmate to death. Georgia executed a woman in 2015.

articles.title_orig: US, Iran separately talk with mediators in latest bid to end war
articles.title_zh: US, Iran separately talk with mediators in latest bid to end war
articles.content_orig:
US official says ‘constructive’ Iran talks continue but nuclear issues delay deal
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has met with Qatari mediators in New York to discuss a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, while a United States official said there would be no agreement to end the war unless Tehran’s nuclear programme is addressed.
Araghchi told Iranian state media on Monday that the Qatari mediators would carry the ideas discussed at the meeting to the US and that he hoped to receive Washington’s final response by Tuesday.
“We talked about ideas and how to find solutions to fulfil Iran’s conditions and how to implement those conditions,” he said. “They had some ideas, and we had a discussion that they will also present to the American side.”
Asked whether he would stay in New York to await the reply, Araghchi said he would fly to Tehran within hours.
“Whenever the Qataris have a response, they know how to get it to us,” he said.
He described the meetings as part of an existing exchange of messages through Qatari and Pakistani mediators, which he said had taken on “a more serious form” since Iran submitted its proposal.
The Iranian plan , announced on Friday at the United Nations General Assembly in New York City, calls on the US to release frozen Iranian funds, lift sanctions and end its naval blockade of Iranian ports. Araghchi said those steps could be completed within four or five days, allowing the strait to reopen and negotiations on a final agreement, including on Iran’s nuclear programme, to begin by the seventh day.
US President Donald Trump, however, rejected the proposal on Saturday, calling it “unacceptable”.
The US official, who spoke to Al Jazeera, said indirect discussions were continuing.
The talks were “positive and constructive”, the official said, but stressed there would be no agreement unless Iran’s nuclear programme is addressed. The official said Trump is willing to relieve sanctions and release Iran’s frozen funds in exchange for progress on nuclear issues.
“Iran has indicated they are flexible on the nuclear issues, but the sides still remain apart on the timing of the commitments and who takes which steps first,” the official said.
The official also expressed scepticism of Iran, saying it had broken the memorandum of understanding signed in June by firing on commercial vessels. Tehran denies the accusation and says it was Washington that broke its commitments by failing to halt Israel’s attacks on Lebanon and by seeking to establish alternate shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran had closed the strait, which handled roughly 20 percent of the world’s oil and gas supplies before the war, shortly after the US and Israel launched their offensive on February 28. Iranian attacks on vessels since have sharply curtailed shipping, and oil prices have risen above $100 a barrel.
Even so, crude exports from major Middle East producers rebounded in September to 12.8 million barrels per day, their highest level since the war began, the Reuters news agency reported, citing data from the maritime intelligence firm Kpler.
That is still well below the 18.8 million bpd exported in February.
Some ships have used the US military-supervised route hugging the coast of Oman, travelling at night with tracking systems off and offloading oil to tankers outside the strait. Admiral Brad Cooper, the head of US Central Command, said on Saturday that American forces had assisted 2,000 transits and more than 1 billion barrels of oil in recent months.
The US has also imposed a blockade on Iranian ports and threatened secondary sanctions against airports and companies that do business with Iranian airlines. The United Arab Emirates, Iraq and Oman have already cancelled related flights.
Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump said US officials had also spoken with mediators but insisted that Washington would prevail.
“We’re going to win,” he said. “It’s going to go pretty quickly.” He added that gas prices would fall once the US won the war.
In Tehran, officials struck a defiant tone.
Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, in a message marking the Iran-Iraq War and Israel’s killing of Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah in 2024, said that the days of foreign domination were over.
“Having suffered painful blows from our valiant combatants and the guardians of the Strait of Hormuz, they [the enemy] dare not venture beyond the Arabian Sea,” Khamenei said in the message carried by Iranian media.
“Whenever they have risked doing so, they have only inflicted harm upon themselves, and the time is fast approaching when the Arabian Sea, too, will be cleared of their presence.”
Major-General Ali Abdollahi, the armed forces chief of staff, meanwhile, warned that Iran and allied forces would deliver a “decisive and devastating response” to any threat against the country.
Rear Admiral Habibollah Sayyari insisted that the Strait of Hormuz remains closed and said Iranian forces were ready to prevent enemy forces from entering the country.

PLYMOUTH, Mass. — Lindsay Clancy's legal team and Massachusetts prosecutors have agreed to delay defense attorney Kevin Reddington’s motion to investigate the lone holdout juror in her mistrial, his attorney Edward Paltzik told Fox News' Kayleigh McEnany Monday.
"The DA and Reddington consent to adjourn the motion to investigate Michael," Paltzik said. "If Judge Sullivan signs an order today, much of it could be adjourned. Either way, a status conference is still likely. But the motion about Michael is likely not on tomorrow."
Clancy attorney Kevin Reddington, however, fired back a short time later in a fiery statement of his own, calling Paltzik's statement "pure nonsense" while conceding that he and county prosecutors had agreed to a continuation as a "professional courtesy" to local counsel now working with the holdout juror.
A final decision is subject to Judge William Sullivan, but the judge has not yet announced a decision one way or the other. The delay agreement comes as the juror's new local counsel informed the parties that he does not have access to impounded information necessary to prepare a response.

As is professional courtesy, both the government and I agreed to continue this specific motion to a later date at their request."

The terms adjourned and continued are similar but have distinct meanings.
"Adjournment generally signifies that something like a hearing is off indefinitely especially because no date is specified," explained retired Massachusetts Judge Carol Erskine. EAGAN, Minn. â Even something believed to be the best decision can be tremendously difficult.
Such is the case for Vikings General Manager Nolan Teasley and Head Coach Kevin O'Connell in opting to trade J.J. McCarthy to the Giants in exchange for a 2027 fifth-round draft pick.
O'Connell called Monday "a tough day," and Teasley emphasized the human aspect of the transaction in their respective press conferences with Twin Cities media members.
"These types of decisions for me are never easy because the person is important," Teasley said. "I think he was an important person to this organization. I enjoyed my time getting to know J.J. I want the best for him, and I hope he succeeds in the future."
O'Connell noted nothing about the business decision changes the way he feels about McCarthy or the "hopes" he has for the 23-year-old quarterback moving forward. He believes New York â who recently lost starting QB Jaxson Dart for the season to a knee injury â presents a favorable opportunity for McCarthy.
"As I told him, I'll be pulling for him like crazy, to see him go and do well and apply a lot of the things we've talked about over his period of time here," O'Connell said.
He emphasized the amount of time he's spent with McCarthy since the Vikings drafted him 10 th overall in 2024.
"I care about him. I have tremendous respect for him as a player, a person," O'Connell said. "I've just had a chance to spend time with him this morning, which was emotional. Our relationship means a lot to me. I believe it means a lot to him, and I was just really thankful to have that time 1-on-1 with him.
"These situations are never easy. From a standpoint of being the head coach, you understand hard decisions in the NFL. I understand them firsthand, going back a long way for me personally," O'Connell continued. "It's always going to be about the relationship. It's always going to be about investing in all these players so much and understanding their families are involved with that."
Below are additional takeaways from Monday's media sessions with Teasley and O'Connell.

1. Timing & return of trade
O'Connell acknowledged the importance of relationships with players and their families while also recognizing the ultimate business of leading a pro team.
"You understand the decisions in the NFL that have to be made in the best interest in the organization," O'Connell said, "and you have a responsibility, and that's why I credit Nolan throughout â¦ just his ability to handle situations with so much tact and thought, always thinking forward on building our team."
Teasley confirmed that McCarthy never requested a trade, but he declined to specify exactly when conversations around a potential transaction began. He did note that this specific situation â timing, scenario and compensation â prompted the trade to happen how and when it did.
"You have to recognize when a different situation or a new opportunity presents itself that it has the opportunity to present better outcomes," Teasley said. "When the situation with the Giants presented itself, we spoke internally â that's coaches, myself, the personnel staff, ownership â everyone came together. Just in terms of where we are and in terms of our roster, where it is currently â¦ and what we might want to do in the future.
"Ultimately, we came to the conclusion that this was the best path forward and the best decision for the Minnesota Vikings," he added.
Teasley later said things "recently came together" to make the trade.
"We got to the point where the return made sense for us now to get an asset that, in all honesty, is going to help us in the future, or it could help us this season," he said. "So to have another asset that can help us continue to build, because the season and this roster [is] going to constantly evolve, and today's another example of that."
2. Exhausted development plan
Considering McCarthy only made 10 starts, O'Connell was asked about the trade through the lens of: Was there anything else that could have been done to bring McCarthy along?
He said the organization emptied the tank in its efforts to develop the 23-year-old.
"We tried to do everything we could to collaborate with a plan for [him] among coaches, among everybody in this building to try to put him in position to develop and grow," the coach said. "And I do think, you know, I do think he did. I do think he did develop and grow.
"And I think he improved. I think he improved this offseason," he added. "But at the same time, you're always going to look inward and look at it [like the] circumstances, they are what they were and are. But what could we have done differently? And J.J. and I talked about that this morning of, you know, like 'Do I wish I took him out of that first preseason game earlier? You know, whatever it may be, like that's where your mind goes, and I think it's a good question."
3. Murray's trajectory & QB room
Minnesota kept four quarterbacks on its initial 53-man roster, achieving its goal of building a deep and competitive room. Without McCarthy, Teasley maintained there's "a lot of belief" in the position.
He cited Kyler Murray's potential in the offense and is "still looking forward to that coming to fruition" after he took some steps forward Sunday in his first full game since October 2025.
Teasley also highlighted Carson Wentz's ability "to step in and win football games" and noted that Max Brosmer's development is important to the organization.
O'Connell elaborated on Murray and the offense trying to mesh.
"Look, we've seen Kyler play 11 snaps in one game and played against a good defense on the road yesterday. There's a lot of things beyond Kyler that we need to improve, including myself, and we're going to do that, and we're going to ascend as an offense," O'Connell said. "I believe in our guys. I believe in where we can get to as a team, and I just love the fact that collectively we're able to come together and find a way to win football games."

China has expanded overseas travel restrictions for top AI professionals in private firms to include the families of key personnel, further tightening measures designed to prevent the outflow of critical know-how and information to the U.S.
Government agencies have recently begun to share the wider restrictions with affected people, which include prominent startup founders as well as the heads of strategically important companies in AI-related fields, people familiar with the matter said. Direct relatives such as spouses and children of certain AI and chip executives, whose work is considered paramount to state security, are now required to obtain approval from Beijing before going abroad even for short trips, the people said.
That marks a broadening of existing curbs on the freedom of movement of China’s most influential tech talent — a category that encompasses entrepreneurs, researchers and executives. While not an outright ban on travel, the new requirement is likely to exert a further chilling effect on a tech sector already facing unprecedented curbs. CBS’ and MTV ‘s coverage of the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards averaged a combined 8.43 million viewers on Sunday night, according to Nielsen Live+same day fast nationals. Those numbers are subject to change once finals are in, but for now that makes it the most-watched VMAs in 11 years (since 2015, when it only ran on MTV) and puts it up 51% vs. last year’s show.
The VMAs were likely assisted by an NFL football overrun (which went late until the Baltimore Ravens defeated the Dallas Cowboys), pushing the start time of the VMAs by several minutes (to 7:51 p.m. ET). The show still started at 4:30 p.m. PT inside L.A. Live’s Peacock Theater, but wound up being tape-delayed as a result on CBS.
That 8.43 million number includes the simulcast on CBS and MTV, as well as an encore on MTV. But in an apples-to-apples comparison, the show last year (on Sept. 7, 2025) also aired on CBS, MTV and encored on MTV — and that telecast brought in 5.60 million viewers.
In individual network numbers, the CBS telecast averaged 7.61 million viewers, up 52% from last year (5.00 million). MTV’s simulcast averaged 686,000 viewers (up 40% from last year’s 481,000). And the MTV encore brought in 142,000 viewers (up 31% from 108,000 last year).
According to CBS, this year repped the best same-day audience for the VMAs since 2015, when the awards show hit a big 12.73 million viewers.
In demos, this was the most-watched VMAs in adults 25-54 (3.11 million) since 2019 (3.55 million) and was up +34% from last year (2.32 million). In adults 18-49, the show took in 2.66 million — the best since 2018 (3.02 million) and up 32% from 2025 (2.02 million). And in adults 18-34, the show averaged 1/09 million, the best since 2020 (1.14 million) and up 46% from last year (751,000).
CBS also reported social highlights: 31.1M interactions and 159M video views (up 8% from last year).
The 2026 VMAs opened with Madonna — in her first VMAs performance in 23 years — with Sabrina Carpenter and Charli XCX. The show also featured Taylor Swift winning the video of the year award, taking the MTV VMA artist director award and premiering her new music video to “Patient Zero.”
Also, Nirvana received the video vanguard award, and tributes were held for Dolly Parton and George Michael. Other performers included GENER8ION, Gunna, Kacey Musgraves, Lisa, Madonna, Raye, Shaboozey, Sienna Spiro, Sombr, Teddy Swims and Yung Lean.
Snoop Dogg hosted the 2026 VMAs. Gunpowder & Sky produced the special, while. Van Toffler served as producer. Jesse Ignjatovic of Den of Thieves, Barb Bialkowski and Bruce Gillmer were executive producers alongside Barry Barclay and Floris Bauer. Melanie Block was co-executive producer and Gary Lanvy as co-producer. Snoop Dogg was executive producer alongside producers Sara Ramaker and Jasmin Ratansi. articles.title_orig: Highlights: SpaceX reaches orbit in unprecedented Starship test flight
articles.title_zh: Highlights: SpaceX reaches orbit in unprecedented Starship test flight
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX launched the company's Super Heavy-Starship on its first flight to orbit Monday — an abbreviated three-hour mission that marked a major step toward perfecting the world's most powerful rocket for commercial flights and NASA moon missions.
One of the Starship upper stage's six Raptor engines shut down early during the climb to an initially suborbital trajectory. After assessing telemetry, Elon Musk's flight control team decided the spacecraft was otherwise healthy and a second engine firing using a single Raptor engine completed the climb to orbit.
Right after that, the Starship upper stage deployed 26 third-generation Starlink internet satellites that will join the company's ever-growing constellation in the first use of the new rocket to launch operational satellites in low-Earth orbit.
After the satellites were away, SpaceX controllers opted to bring the Starship back to Earth well ahead of schedule, ending the mission three hours after launch with a Pacific Ocean splashdown north of Hawaii just before noon EDT.
For NASA, getting the Starship into orbit and back are critical steps on the road to perfecting the system in time to support a planned Artemis moon landing , using a variant of the Starship, in 2028.
A future moon mission will require multiple Super Heavy-Starship tanker flights to fuel the lander for its flight to the moon before docking with a NASA Orion crew capsule in lunar orbit, picking up two astronauts and carrying them down to the surface and back.
"Congrats @SpaceX !," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a post on the social media platform X. "Gorgeous launch, getting Ship to orbit and managing every step in a safe, responsible, and especially inspirational way. @NASA , along with the rest of the interested public, is excited to help where we can and for Starship missions to become routine!"
Few doubt SpaceX will eventually get the Super Heavy-Starship flying reliably, but it's not yet known whether the company will be able to meet NASA's ambitious 2028 target date for the Artemis IV moon landing.
Monday's mission got off to a spectacular start. The Super Heavy booster's 33 methane-burning Raptor engines ignited with a rush of flame at 8:49 a.m. EDT, quickly propelling the 400-foot-tall rocket away from SpaceX's Starbase launch site on the Texas Gulf Coast.
The Super Heavy first stage booster, generating some 16 million pounds of thrust — twice the power of NASA's Space Launch System moon rocket — rapidly accelerated as it consumed propellant and lost weight, climbing out of the thick lower atmosphere along a southeasterly trajectory. One of the engines shut down early, but the Super Heavy was designed to reach space despite the loss of one or two engines.
Two minutes and 20 seconds after liftoff, the rest of the first stage engines began shutting down while the six Raptors powering the Starship upper stage began firing up in a "hot staging" maneuver seconds before the booster separated and fell away.
While the Starship continued toward space, the Super Heavy booster flipped around, restarted its engines to reverse course and then flew itself back to the Texas Gulf Coast. A second engine apparently shut down early during the so-called boost-back burn, but the huge rocket was able to execute a seemingly normal vertical splashdown a few miles off shore.
During the most recent previous test flight, three engines suffered problems that prevented a full-duration boost-back burn and only eight of 13 engines fired for the landing burn. The result was a "hard" splashdown. SpaceX implemented multiple upgrades and software changes to ensure a successful return this time around.
The first stage is designed to be captured by giant mechanical arms on its launch gantry, a feat SpaceX has accomplished four times to date. But until upgrades and improvements have been tested, SpaceX has opted to stick with ocean splashdowns as a safety precaution. The Starship upper stage also is designed to be captured back at the pad after a trip to space and back, but that milestone has not yet been attempted.
The Starship upper stage launched Monday climbed into a 180-mile-high orbit with two engine firings. The first, ending a minute after the booster's splashdown, was intended to put the Starship onto a sub-orbital trajectory similar to past flights that would result in a safe splashdown even if SpaceX lost control of the rocket.
Despite the premature shutdown of one engine, the Starship was cleared to proceed with the orbit-insertion burn and eight-and-a-half minutes after that, a Pez-like dispenser in the rocket's nose began launching 26 third-generation Starlink internet satellites, each with 10 times the capacity of the previous generation.
The mission was initially expected to last six orbits, leading to a splashdown off the coast of Chile around 6:40 p.m. But with the Starlink satellites safely on their way, mission managers opted to bring the ship down early with a Pacific Ocean splashdown north of Hawaii.
As with earlier test flights, the Starship fell back into the discernible atmosphere belly-first, rapidly slowing in a fireball of electrically charged plasma before using its fins and flaps to control its orientation during the descent.
As the ship neared the ocean, three Raptor's re-ignited, the spacecraft flipped up to vertical and settled to a controlled, tail first splashdown in the Pacific Ocean at 11:57 a.m. EDT.
As is usually the case with ocean splashdowns, the rocket tipped over, fell onto its side and exploded as residual propellants ignited.
SpaceX currently has two Super Heavy-Starship pads at its Starbase facility in Texas and three more under construction in Florida, including one at historic pad 39A at the Kennedy Space Center and the others at the adjacent Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. SpaceX plans its initial launch from Florida late this year or early next.
And multiple pads will be needed.
SpaceX is building a variant of the Starship to serve as a lander for Artemis astronauts. For moon missions, the company will need to launch up to 15 or so Super Heavy-Starship tankers to refuel the company's lunar lander before it can head for the moon to await the arrival of astronauts in a Lockheed Martin-built Orion capsule.
From there, the 165-foot-tall lander will carry two crew members down to the surface, landing vertically near the moon's south pole. The astronauts then will ride an external elevator down to the surface and back up again when their exploration is complete.
With the first such landing targeted for 2028, SpaceX must ramp up its Super Heavy-Starship test schedule to get the vehicle certified for human spaceflight and to demonstrate the reliability required to safely launch more than a dozen tankers within days of the lander's launch.
Many observers with past experience at NASA and elsewhere in the aerospace industry doubt SpaceX can deliver a tested "human landing system" Starship variant by 2028. NASA is hedging its bets, funding development of an alternative lander designed by Blue Origin.
During a test flight in low Earth orbit next year — Artemis III — NASA plans to launch four astronauts in an Orion capsule who will attempt to rendezvous and dock with prototype landers launched separately by SpaceX and Blue Origin.

articles.title_orig: Experts worry about Nvidia’s AI chip sales in China and influence over Trump
articles.title_zh: Experts worry about Nvidia’s AI chip sales in China and influence over Trump
articles.content_orig:
On its face, the recent summit between Donald Trump and China’s president Xi Jinping didn’t change much in the world of AI regulation. Export controls were not discussed, with neither country seemingly interested in making concessions. An already tenuous trade truce was temporarily extended for just two months, and looming US controls that could drop soon could easily end that and trigger China to retaliate by cutting off exports of rare earths, analysts expect.
However, in the background of these shaky talks, Nvidia appeared to notch a big win, as China is currently mulling relaxing controls and allowing some of its biggest AI firms to import perhaps millions more of Nvidia’s banned chips over the next year.
Sources familiar with China’s talks told The Information that China’s tech oversight arm, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, asked Alibaba and ByteDance to share plans to buy Nvidia’s RTX Pro 5500 chips. Although these are gaming chips, China asked firms to detail how they plan to use them, with expectations that chips could be put into servers to help power the country’s most in-demand AI models.
Increasingly, Trump looks to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang for advice on AI, but not everybody agrees that what’s good for Nvidia is good for the United States.
Already the world’s most valuable company, Nvidia would obviously profit enormously in a world where risks are downplayed, and both countries’ priorities remain powering rapid developments in frontier AI without pumping the brakes. Some critics worry that Nvidia’s profit motivations may be steering Trump’s thinking at a pivotal moment when it may matter how well a president actually understands the risks of a new technology.
For Nvidia, a big goal since Trump took office was to open up more of China’s market so that Nvidia could start selling chips that were restricted during Joe Biden’s administration. Huang has blamed US export controls for cutting Nvidia’s share of China’s advanced AI chip market from about 95 percent to zero, The Information reported .
Trump was not an instant ally. Instead, he came into office asking “What the hell is Nvidia?” and rather than loosening Biden’s export controls, he initially tightened them further, most notably by banning exports of H200 chips to China. Trump was even thinking about breaking Nvidia up, expecting that stoking more competition among chipmakers domestically was crucial to America winning the so-called “AI race” with China .
But then he met Huang over dinner at Mar-a-Lago, where Trump said he “learned the facts of life” and understood that Nvidia as a firm is an “amazing” AI leader. Ignoring warnings from lawmakers and national security experts, Trump lifted the export controls on H200 chips , which China eventually allowed to be sold to some firms. Since then, Trump and Huang have appeared together in public repeatedly, and they regularly talk by phone, according to Stephen Witt, the author of The Thinking Machine: Jensen Huang, Nvidia, And The World’s Most Coveted Microchip .
In an interview discussing Huang’s influence over Trump, Witt told NPR that Trump’s recent claims—suggesting that it’s a “hoax” that AI might destroy humanity and that instead AI will be an economic boon—are “exactly Jensen’s talking points.”
“Jensen is now the president’s most influential adviser on technology issues,” Witt said. “The two have become quite close.”
Witt spent time with “tons” of people in the AI industry who share Huang’s views, he told NPR. And like Huang, they tended to downplay risks that software developers—including Nvidia’s biggest customers like Anthropic and OpenAI —are right now urging the White House to take seriously, he found.
“Most of the hardware people, most of the people who designed the networking equipment and the microchips, feel like Jensen does,” Witt said. “They tend to have a very low sense of risk regarding this technology. They just don’t see it.”
He said this debate has been going on between the two camps for the past 10 years and “neither camp has moved at all.” With Huang growing closer to Trump, it seems likely the president will continue downplaying leading AI firms’ warnings and avoiding serious talks with China about their models’ risks. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed ahead of Trump’s talks with Xi that “the president is completely aligned with Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia.”
According to The Information, China lifting export curbs on Nvidia’s gaming chips “would give Nvidia perhaps its best chance in more than a year to regain some momentum in China’s AI market.” If China gives the nod, ByteDance plans to order 1 million chips, which would automatically secure for Nvidia two quarters of projected sales.
That would certainly help improve Nvidia’s financial outlook in China, as China’s delayed approval of H200 sales meant sales were dismal, comprising less than 1 percent of Nvidia’s data center revenue in the most recent quarter.
Andrew Yoon, a researcher at an AI safety nonprofit called CivAI, told CNBC that in the AI industry, “Nvidia is the most aggressive in terms of, let’s just make money.”
“At every turn, they are really trying to just make sure whatever happens is good for Nvidia’s bottom line,” Yoon said.
If the US and China continue to loosen controls, some experts fear that too many chips may end up being diverted to China. Eventually, that could cause US data centers to lose a precious domestic chip supply that’s currently making it possible to stay ahead on frontier AI, the thinking goes.
Nvidia’s reporting suggests that as of now, the countries don’t compete for resources, though. In the first half of 2026, Nvidia reportedly took a $400 million hit due to vast quantities of unsold H200 chips. No American firms want those chips, since they can access Nvidia’s more advanced chips.
However, demand for chips made for China’s market could perhaps change, as more US data centers come online, policy experts believe .
Nvidia’s spokesperson told Ars that China lifting curbs on “outdated” gaming chips “released nearly a half a decade ago” will only benefit US firms unfairly burdened by restrictions on chips that cannot be used to train AI. The statement recalls Huang’s remarks at a recent “All-In” summit hosted by Trump’s former AI czar David Sacks. Huang publicly promised Trump that “we’re going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race of America. Every industry, every company, every state, every people.”
Yet, Witt joked that “Jensen is really the only one who wants to sell his equipment to China.”
Witt thinks that a responsible US president would set up a group like the National Transportation Safety Board to review mandatory reports of AI safety incidents. That could support the US-China safety alert system announced last week, which right now troublingly includes no tech experts. But that likely won’t happen since “Jensen has convinced Trump that what’s good for Nvidia is good for America,” Witt said.
It remains unclear if China will approve the gaming chip sales, but sources told The Information that the government intends to allow at least some into the country. The pressure may be on to approve them since “Chinese companies are rolling out AI products and services faster than they can ﬁnd the chips to run them,” The Information noted. At least one buyer “plans to put eight RTX Pro 5500s in each server, a standard setup that lets the chips work together on larger AI models,” sources said. Supposedly, Nvidia’s preparing to ship the first orders this December.
If Huang gets his way, Chinese firms will buy millions more of Nvidia’s chips in the coming years, helping the firm maintain global dominance over companies that are locked in on advancing AI.
During the most recent summit between Trump and Xi, Huang joined many US tech leaders at a state dinner, including Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Sam Altman, Mark Zuckerberg, and Satya Nadella. Noticeably, China invited none of its tech leaders.

articles.title_orig: Trump administration cannot tie anti-terrorism grants to election security, judge rules
articles.title_zh: Trump administration cannot tie anti-terrorism grants to election security, judge rules
articles.content_orig:
A judge on Monday vacated a Trump administration rule that would withhold 20% of federal counterterrorism funds allocated for states unless states and certain municipalities made certain changes to how they administer elections.
In his ruling , U.S. District Court Judge Amir Ali said the Federal Emergency Management Agency exceeded its legal authority "by conditioning the counterterrorism grant funds on changes to routine election administration."
Ali also said FEMA , a division of the Department of Homeland Security , had not shown how the desired changes to election administration related to stopping terrorism.
Ali's decision in Washington, D.C., came in response to a lawsuit challenging FEMA's new rule, filed in August by counties in Texas and Tennessee, and the city of Columbus, Ohio.
The Brennan Center for Justice at New York University , which represents some of the plaintiffs in the suit against FEMA and DHS, said on Aug. 17 that FEMA's conditions "violate the Constitution, jeopardize public safety, and put election security at risk."
"Over the last two years, courts have largely blocked the administration's repeated attempts to seize congressional and state authority over elections," the Brennan Center said at the time.  "Now, DHS is holding public safety funding hostage in order to coerce states and local governments into adopting some of the very policies that the administration has tried and failed to impose."
The Brennan Center said the funds that stood to be withheld if FEMA's conditions were allowed to remain in place totaled tens of millions of dollars.
A spokesman for the Department of Justice, which represented DHS and FEMA, declined to comment on Ali's ruling.
Abbie Kamin, the County Attorney of Harris County, Texas, said in a statement, "Today's win is the result of cities and counties standing together against blatant federal overreach that jeopardized public safety."
"The court agreed that holding public safety funding hostage to force the president's agenda is dangerous and illegal," said Kamin, whose county was one of the plaintiffs in the case. "Under our laws, states and localities control our elections, and today's ruling reaffirms that."
FEMA issued the rule in June requiring states "and their respective high-risk urban areas" to make certain changes to election administration or face the withholding of 20% of a state's allocation of counterterrorism funds from the federal government, Ali noted.
Urban areas in the U.S. vote overwhelmingly for Democrats.
The changes include submitting a plan for transitioning from electronic voting systems that use bar codes or QR codes to hand-marked paper ballots; conducting, under federally specified guidelines, a post-election manual audit of 5% of the ballots; and ensuring that each election jurisdiction reconciles the number of voters who voted in a federal election to the number of ballots cast.
The required changes also include verifying the U.S. citizenship of all voters in the state's registration database, and the citizenship of poll workers, election administrators and election-system vendors.
Ali, in his ruling, said, "FEMA's conditions here — which are imposed on states and localities at their own expense, rather than funded by grants, and which address routine election administration decisions rather than the types of terrorist act threats contemplated by the statute — go beyond what Congress authorized."
"For example, the defendants say the ... condition requiring states to adopt FEMA's proposed citizenship-verification procedures in maintaining lists of registered voters 'ensures that only U.S. citizens are voting in U.S. elections,'" Ali wrote.
"But it never explains how that condition, or any of the others, is tied to the goal of shoring up vulnerabilities to terrorist attacks," the judge said.

articles.title_orig: Justice Alito Recuses Himself Days Before Major Climate-Change Case
articles.title_zh: Justice Alito Recuses Himself Days Before Major Climate-Change Case
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — Conservative Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito will no longer participate in a major climate change case after facing calls that he recuse himself because of his stock holdings in oil companies.
The new development was disclosed in a letter dated Monday and sent to lawyers involved in the case, with no reason given.
“Justice Alito has determined that he will not continue to participate in this case,” the letter said.
Alito had, via a court spokeswoman, previously told NBC News there was no need for him to step aside from the case, which is being argued next week and could have broad nationwide implications when the court issues a ruling.
Left-leaning groups have repeatedly called for Alito’s recusal from the case, in which ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy are seeking to toss out a Colorado lawsuit seeking damages from the oil companies for the impacts of climate change.
Although Alito does not own stocks in either company, he does hold stocks in oil companies ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66, as well as five other firms involved in the energy sector, his financial disclosure report says.
Activists calling for his recusal said the companies he holds stocks in could benefit if the Supreme Court throws out the Colorado case, brought by the city and county of Boulder, because it could directly affect similar cases across the country in which they are among the defendants.
The court has a 6-3 conservative majority. With Alito stepping aside, it raises the possibility of a 4-4 split, which would leave the major legal issues unresolved.
The oil and gas industry is hoping the court will issue a broad ruling that would prevent cases like the one in Colorado from moving forward in state courts, potentially saving it from paying out billions of dollars in damages.
Earlier in the litigation, in 2023, Alito did recuse himself when the court turned away an appeal from the companies in the Colorado case.
On the same day, the court rejected appeals in similar cases involving other companies, including ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66. Alito also did not participate in those cases.
In May, a court spokesman said Alito had “inadvertently recused” in the earlier Colorado case.
“Justice Alito does not have a financial interest in any party” involved in the case, the court spokeswoman said in a statement provided to NBC News at the time. Alito was advised by the court’s legal counsel that “his recusal is not required,” she added.
That was before the most recent calls for Alito to step aside based on the indirect benefit he could obtain from a ruling in favor of Exxon and Suncor.
Earlier this month, an advocacy group called Consumer Watchdog pointed to disclosures made by ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66 to shareholders in which they warned of the risks the companies face as a result of climate lawsuits making similar claims to the Colorado case.
“Justice Alito’s recusal ... is the right decision, and one he should have made from the start,” Alexandra Nagy, the group’s organizing director, said in a statement.
The Supreme Court spokeswoman did not immediately respond to a request seeking further comment.
Some conservatives have also pushed for liberal Justice Elena Kagan to recuse herself in the case because of a controversy over a chapter on climate change included in, and subsequently removed from , a reference manual for judges. Kagan wrote a brief foreword to the manual and recently told lawmakers that she never read the chapter in question.
Lawrence Hurley is a senior Supreme Court reporter for NBC News.
